checks.check: All protected routes have authentication (middleware / route guard)
All non-public routes must be intercepted — no route is accidentally exposed without auth middleware
Sensitive data read/write has authorization (RLS / DAL / policy engine)
No client-trusted identity parameters without server-side verification (`userId`, `orgId`, `shopId`)
Payment/webhook flows have idempotency (using provider event ID or equivalent)
API responses do not leak internal info (stack traces, internal paths, secret fragments)
Security/authorization/integrity checks fail closed when they cannot establish permission or validity; optional diagnostics may fail without blocking unrelated authorized work.
Deployable dependency sets are reproducible through the ecosystem’s adopted lock/pinning mechanism; assess lockfile applicability for libraries and dependency-free projects.
Hash verification of dependencies — dependency integrity verified via hash/checksum, not just version pinning
No long-lived credentials where short-lived identity is possible
External writes have audit trail (`user_id` + `timestamp` + `trace_id`)
Automation systems have emergency stop / kill switch mechanism
High-risk operations follow the adopted approval controls, including two-party approval where required; document and enforce any authorized emergency path.
Critical financial/auth/deletion audit records have the required tamper resistance and retention; use WORM or another mechanism meeting the adopted integrity contract.
For the actual deployment, apply least-privilege network access and required ingress/egress restrictions or zone isolation.
Where dependencies are deployed, assess and wire vulnerability auditing appropriate to the project’s risk and CI environment; verify the scanner actually runs.
Production database writes use authorized service/operator paths with least privilege and auditability; routine human dashboards must not bypass application controls.
Sensitive exposed endpoints have abuse/rate controls appropriate to their authentication, payment or administrative risk.
Where dependency inventory is required for deployment, compliance or incident response, generate a usable SBOM or equivalent verified inventory through the build.
Security incident response has documented ownership and usable procedures appropriate to the deployment and its recovery obligations.
Where storage buckets exist, verify intended public/private access and periodic review appropriate to exposure risk.
For deployed IaC/container surfaces, wire applicable infrastructure/image security checks according to the project’s threat and delivery model.
Dependency update rollout matches failure impact and recovery needs; use staged deployment where required rather than imposing it on every package change.
Authentication policy has a consistent owner across entrypoints, using shared wrappers or an equivalent mechanism that prevents policy drift.
Each service has its own identity with fine-grained permissions rather than sharing a broad credential.

anti_patterns: Security/authorization failure handlers continue a protected operation without establishing permission
Client-trusted identity parameters without server-side verification
Unnecessarily long-lived credentials despite a supported shorter-lived mechanism appropriate to this host and threat model
No kill switch for privileged automation
Privileged writes with no audit trail
Secret material present in repo or unvalidated runtime paths
